subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
subtype: Approach: putting the event in perspective with a mentor [Thinking]
passage:
Jyoti found Ramesh alone in the pantry, staring at a cold cup of tea.
"Rough week?" Jyoti asked.
"I keep thinking I'm not cut out for this," Ramesh said. "The wrong file went to the client. Everyone was nice about it. That's worse."
"Want to hear something? Early in my career, I switched off the payroll server the night before salary day. By accident. Two hundred people, no pay."
"What did you do?"
"Told my boss within the hour. We fixed it by midnight. I wrote to everyone the next morning, and nobody lost a single rupee."
"And you kept the job?"
"I got more responsibility. What mattered was how I fixed it."
Ramesh looked at the tea, and then finally drank it.

qa.q: What did Jyoti switch off the night before salary day?
qa.a: Jyoti switched off the payroll server.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling when Jyoti came into the pantry?
qa.a: Ramesh was ashamed and doubtful, thinking about not being cut out for this and unsettled by people's kindness.

qa.q: What could Ramesh do this week to show that the mistake is fixable?
qa.a: Ramesh could write a short note on how the wrong file went out and what changes will stop it, and share it with the team.

qa.q: How might Jyoti have felt while telling the payroll story?
qa.a: Jyoti probably remembered the fear of that night and wanted to spare Ramesh from carrying it alone.

grounding: The dialogue shows a senior colleague sharing a similar past mistake and how it was handled, so the employee sees the error as fixable and recovery as more important than perfection.

subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
subtype: Approach: putting the event in perspective with a mentor [Thinking]
passage:
I'm Trisha, and three weeks after I broke the payment page for four hours, I still couldn't look at my own code without feeling sick. Irfan, our senior architect, took me for tea on the office terrace. I thought he was going to warn me.
Instead he said, 'Did you know I once took down the whole mobile app for a day? I pushed a config file with a missing bracket.' He laughed, not at me, at himself. 'My manager made me write the fix and the review. Then she gave me the next big release.'
I asked what he had learnt. He thought about it. 'That the mistake is one day. How you recover is the next ten years.'
I went back to my desk and opened the review document I had been avoiding. It was just a bug. A fixable one.

qa.q: What did Irfan push that took down the mobile app?
qa.a: A config file with a missing bracket.

qa.q: How did Trisha feel before the tea, and how did that change?
qa.a: Trisha felt sick and ashamed about the mistake, then calmer and able to see it as fixable after Irfan's story.

qa.q: What else could Trisha do to turn the mistake into learning?
qa.a: Trisha could finish the review, suggest one safeguard, and later share the story with newer engineers, as Irfan did.

qa.q: Why might Irfan choose to share his own mistake?
qa.a: Irfan probably remembers how heavy it felt and wants Trisha to see that recovery matters more than a perfect record.

grounding: It shows a senior colleague sharing a similar old mistake so the employee sees the error as fixable and that recovery matters more than perfection.

subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
subtype: Approach: putting the event in perspective with a mentor [Thinking]
passage:
Team lead's note, 9 August.
Irfan has been quiet since the billing error last week, when a rate he entered overcharged forty customers. He has apologised three times. On Wednesday I asked Asif, who has been here twelve years, to have lunch with him.
Asif told me afterwards what he had shared: in his second year he sent the wrong price file to every branch, and the company lost a week of sales. He had wanted to resign. His manager told him, 'Fix it, learn it, stay.'
This morning Irfan came to me with a one-page note: what went wrong, a proposed rate-check step, and a line at the bottom: 'I'll be the reviewer for rate changes next quarter.' He looked steadier. I've accepted his proposal and will check in with him in two weeks.

qa.q: How many customers did the rate Irfan entered overcharge?
What does Irfan offering to be the reviewer suggest about how he feels now?
qa.a: It suggests he feels steadier and more hopeful, seeing the error as something to learn from rather than only to be ashamed of.

qa.q: Why did the team lead ask Asif to have lunch with Irfan instead of giving advice directly?
qa.a: A colleague who made a bigger mistake and stayed can show Irfan, better than any advice, that recovery is possible.

qa.q: What was it like for Asif to share his old mistake?
qa.a: Asif once wanted to resign over it, so telling the story may have been a little uncomfortable but also meaningful, passing on what his own manager gave him.

grounding: It shows a team lead's note on an employee helped by a senior colleague's story of a similar mistake to see the error as fixable.
